hammack-bond-yields-fiscal-path.headline: Fed's Hammack warns bond-yield rise reflects 'unsustainable' fiscal path and AI capex demand
hammack-bond-yields-fiscal-path.body_md:
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack told a conference at her own bank on September 25 that the recent climb in long-term Treasury yields is not the kind of thing the Fed can simply cut its way out of. Real interest rates, she said, have risen faster than inflation expectations — a distinction that matters, because it points to demand for capital and worries about government borrowing rather than a loss of faith that the Fed will eventually tame prices.

"We're reasonably well anchored from an inflation expectations perspective," Hammack said, according to Bloomberg's account of the remarks. But she was blunter about the other side of the ledger: "The US is on an unsustainable fiscal path."

![Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/Beth_M._Hammack.jpg)

## Two forces, one yield curve

The 10-year Treasury yield has pushed to around 5.17%, its highest since mid-2007, while the 30-year has traded near 5.47%, with an intraday print of 5.501% — a level last seen in 2004. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates have followed, drifting back toward 7%.

Hammack's framing split the causes into two buckets. One is fiscal: persistent federal deficits mean the Treasury keeps auctioning more debt into a market that is demanding more compensation to hold it. The other is corporate, and newer — the financing needs of the artificial-intelligence buildout. "Demand for investment linked to AI is competing for capital in the bond market," she said, adding that "longer-term questions remain over how AI could affect inflation."

The scale involved explains why she raised it. Global AI-linked bond issuance is on pace to approach $570 billion in 2026, roughly four times last year's rate over the same stretch, as hyperscalers—Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle—commit a combined $700–725 billion to capital spending this year. Nomura has estimated that big tech borrowing now equals roughly a quarter of the Treasury's net issuance of notes and bonds to private investors, up fivefold from 2025. The six largest tech companies account for an estimated 8.6% of duration-weighted US investment-grade credit outstanding — data centers, chips and power infrastructure are long-lived assets, and hyperscalers are financing them with long-dated debt that competes directly with Treasuries for the same pool of investors.

## A hawk who now has a vote

Hammack's diagnosis carries more weight than it might have a year ago, because she is a voting member of the FOMC in 2026 and has already used that vote once to push against the consensus. At the July 28–29 meeting she dissented in favor of raising the federal funds rate, arguing inflation had run too high for too long and that the committee needed to act to speed its return to the 2% target. She was careful this week to separate her own analysis from the Fed's job: "the Fed is the decision maker on monetary policy," she said, even as she stays "mindful of financial conditions."

![Fed Chair Kevin Warsh](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/37/Official_portrait_of_Kevin_M._Warsh.jpg)

Her remarks also land inside a changed Fed. Kevin Warsh was confirmed as chair in a bruising 54-45 Senate vote in May and took the gavel from Jerome Powell on May 22, arriving with a reputation for tighter inflation discipline than his predecessor. A Fed led by a self-described inflation hawk, with a hawkish regional president holding a vote, is a different animal from the one markets spent 2024 and 2025 pricing for steady cuts.

## What it means for the rate path

The practical point of Hammack's remarks is that some of the upward pressure on yields sits outside the Fed's control. If deficits and AI-related borrowing keep drawing on the same pool of savings, long-term rates can stay elevated even if the Fed lowers its short-term policy rate — a decoupling that would blunt the transmission of any easing into mortgage costs, corporate borrowing and the rest of the real economy. That is a structural argument, not a cyclical one, and it is harder to solve with monetary policy alone.

The next test comes at the FOMC's October 27–28 meeting, where futures markets will be watching whether Hammack's caution finds allies or stays a minority view. Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement, due in the same window, will show whether the government's own issuance plans add to the supply pressure she flagged — or whether Washington starts treating the fiscal side of the equation as urgently as the market already has.

hsbc-returns-india-broking.headline: HSBC plans return to India equity broking after 13-year absence
hsbc-returns-india-broking.body_md:
HSBC is rebuilding a business it dismantled 13 years ago. The London-headquartered bank is hiring senior staff for cash-equities and institutional broking in India and could relaunch retail broking within months, according to people familiar with the plans — a reversal of its 2013 decision to shut the unit and cut roughly 300 jobs.

![HSBC's building in Fort, Mumbai](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/HSBC_building%2C_Fort%2C_Mumbai.jpg)

> **In one sentence:** HSBC is rebuilding cash-equities and institutional broking staff in India to capture the country's retail-investor IPO boom.

## Why now

The economics that drove HSBC out of Indian broking in 2013 — thin volumes, price wars among discount brokers, a retail base that barely traded — have inverted. India added 23.77 million demat accounts in the twelve months to August 2026, taking the total past 237 million, with roughly 3.27 million opened in August alone, the strongest single month since January. Mainboard IPOs climbed from 80 to 109 in the past fiscal year, raising ₹1.77 trillion ($20bn-plus), and bankers including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan expect the pipeline — headlined by anticipated listings such as Jio Platforms and the National Stock Exchange — to keep running through 2026.

HSBC already holds a dormant broking licence through its subsidiary HSBC InvestDirect Securities (India), which it plans to use rather than apply for a fresh one — the fastest route back into a market it once decided wasn't worth the compliance overhead.

## What the bank is actually rebuilding

The hiring is split between two functions: cash equities, which handles execution and trading for clients, and institutional broking, which serves large domestic and foreign funds rather than individual investors. Retail broking, aimed at India's newly minted demat-account holders, is the piece likely to follow — HSBC is reportedly looking at a largely digital, phone-based offering rather than the branch-heavy model it ran before 2013.

That earlier operation collapsed under its own cost base: HSBC's retail brokerage and depository arm was closed in 2013 with roughly 300 job losses, part of a wider retreat by foreign banks — Citibank, Standard Chartered and Deutsche Bank among them — into narrow institutional-only coverage. HSBC is now the largest foreign bank in India by balance sheet and has been expanding its affluent and wealth-management footprint there, including approval this year to add 20 branches, taking its network to 46.

## Not the only one back at the table

HSBC isn't alone in reconsidering an exit it once thought was permanent. Barclays shut its Indian equities business around 2016 after a late, costly entry into a fee-compressed market, and has separately been preparing to restart equity capital markets coverage there roughly a decade on. The pattern points less to any single bank's strategy shift than to a market that foreign lenders spent the 2010s writing off as unprofitable — and that retail money has since made too large to ignore.

## What to watch

The test now is execution rather than intent: whether HSBC's retail broking product actually launches on the timeline sources describe — "within the next few months" — and whether it can compete on price against domestic discount brokers that built their entire model around the retail volumes HSBC is chasing. India's IPO calendar for the remainder of 2026, and whether the current wave of new demat accounts converts into sustained trading activity rather than one-off subscriptions, will shape how much of that retail opportunity is still on the table by the time HSBC is ready to serve it.

uk-consumer-confidence-weakens.headline: UK consumer confidence weakens ahead of Autumn Budget, BRC warns
uk-consumer-confidence-weakens.body_md:
British households turned markedly gloomier about the economy and their own finances this month, according to the British Retail Consortium's latest sentiment tracker — a shift that has handed the Treasury an unwelcome data point three weeks out from the Autumn Budget.

The BRC's Consumer Sentiment Monitor, compiled with Opinium from a poll of 2,000 UK adults conducted between 8 and 11 September, found expectations for the state of the economy over the next three months fell to -34, down from -28 in August. That snapped four consecutive months of improvement. Sentiment on personal finances weakened almost as sharply, dropping to -15 from -9. Expectations for retail spending eased to +5 from +8, while expected household saving slipped to -7 from -5. Overall spending intentions held flat at +15.

![A "Sale up to 50% off" storefront on Oxford Street, London, with shoppers passing by](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/46/Warehouse_store%2C_Oxford_Street%2C_London%2C_March_2016_01.jpg)

## A four-month run broken

The scale of the reversal is what stands out. Confidence had been climbing steadily since the spring, and the September survey marks the first monthly decline since that run began. The BRC said the drop was sharper among women respondents, and linked the shift to two converging pressures: household bills rising faster than shop prices, and consumers bracing for a jump in energy costs this winter. That combination — squeezed budgets now, a known cost shock arriving in a few months — is doing more to unsettle sentiment than any single data release could on its own.

> "Consumer confidence in the economy stumbled after four months of improvement, with a similar trend for sentiment around personal finances," said Helen Dickinson, the BRC's chief executive. "With the Budget looming large, consumers want to see Government prioritise bringing down the cost of living. Retail will play its part, but the Chancellor must not compound the triple blow from escalating employment costs, energy bills, and business rates."

## Budget options narrow

The BRC's ask is specific: a freeze on the business rates multiplier, so retailers are not forced into a further round of price rises to cover higher property taxes, alongside relief on employment costs and energy bills. The framing matters for the Treasury's room to manoeuvre. A government already navigating a tight fiscal position now faces a retail lobby and a household survey both pointing the same direction — toward measures that visibly protect disposable income rather than ones aimed primarily at investment or long-term growth.

That narrows the Chancellor's options less through arithmetic than through politics. A Budget seen to ignore deteriorating household sentiment carries its own risk, regardless of what the fiscal headroom permits.

## What it means for positioning

For traders, the read-through is toward consumer discretionary weakness rather than a broader recession call — spending intentions overall were flat, and the retail-spending expectation, while down, stayed positive at +5. But the divergence between resilient headline spending and falling confidence in the details (personal finance, saving, the economic outlook) is the kind of gap that typically shows up first in discretionary categories — clothing, homewares, big-ticket items — before it reaches food and essentials. UK defensive and staples-heavy retail names look better insulated than general merchandisers exposed to discretionary swings.

The next checkpoint is the Budget itself, expected within weeks, where the size and shape of any business-rates or cost-of-living measures will show whether the government has taken the BRC's warning as a genuine constraint or a lobbying position to be weighed against other priorities. The BRC's October sentiment reading, likely due in the second half of that month, will be the first indication of whether the Budget moved the needle — or whether the slide continues into the crucial pre-Christmas trading period.

dior-arnault-restructuring.headline: Christian Dior board backs Arnault family's €469m restructuring offer
dior-arnault-restructuring.body_md:
Christian Dior SE's board met on September 23 and set in motion a restructuring that will, by year's end, fold one of the world's largest luxury conglomerates more tightly into a single family's hands. The board did not so much approve a finished deal as clear the runway for one: it convened an ad hoc committee to appoint an independent expert who will rule on the fairness of a cash offer worth an illustrative €469.05 a share — a plan the Arnault family group had unveiled hours earlier as the next step in a multi-year simplification of its holding structure.

The mechanics are dense but the intent is plain. Financière Agache, the family's top holding vehicle, will be merged into Agache, which will then be absorbed into Christian Dior SE itself. Dior will convert into a *société en commandite par actions* — a limited partnership with shares — and take the Agache name. The result collapses a stack of intermediate holding companies into one listed entity through which the Arnault family will control LVMH.

![Bernard Arnault](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Bernard_Arnault_%283%29_-_2017_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## The numbers behind the offer

The family already controls 97.10% of Dior's voting rights through Financière Agache, which leaves a free float of just 2.44% — the slice of shares the family group is now obliged, under French takeover rules, to bid for in cash. The illustrative €469.05 price is pegged at 95% of Dior's net asset value of €493.74, itself derived from a one-month volume-weighted average of LVMH's share price. That works out to a 27.3% premium over Dior's close the day before the announcement, though the final price will float with LVMH's stock and won't be fixed until five business days before the extraordinary general meetings expected in December.

Dior shares jumped as much as 17% on the news — a sharp move for a stock whose free float is small enough that even modest buying pressure moves it, and a signal that remaining minority holders see the tender as a clean exit at a fair markup. Notably, the family says it will not squeeze out holders who decline: those who prefer to stay will keep their shares in the merged Agache SCA rather than being forced out, with the tender offer itself expected to open in the first quarter of 2027 pending clearance from the AMF, France's markets regulator.

## Ownership, tidied; control, entrenched

Strip away the corporate-law scaffolding and the effect is consolidation. The family currently holds 50.33% of LVMH's share capital and 66.27% of its voting rights, routed through Financière Agache and Dior. Once the merger completes, that stake will run through the single listed Agache SCA, holding 49.76% of LVMH's capital and 65.55% of its votes — a broadly similar economic position, but housed in one vehicle instead of several, and structured as a partnership that keeps ownership and management legally distinct. Bernard Arnault and Agache Commandité retain general-partner status, meaning day-to-day control of the empire stays with him regardless of how the capital is eventually divided among his five children.

That detail points to the real driver here: succession. Bylaw changes have already lifted the age limit for Arnault's leadership roles to 85, and he has said he intends to remain in charge for another seven or eight years before handing over — a transition the partnership structure is built to make orderly rather than contested. Consolidating the holding company now, while Arnault is still setting the terms, is standard practice for family-controlled conglomerates managing a generational handoff; it is harder to negotiate governance rights after control has already passed.

The timing carries its own footnote. LVMH shares have lagged this year alongside the broader luxury sector, and the group recently slipped behind L'Oréal in market capitalisation on the Paris exchange — a reminder that even Europe's largest listed conglomerate is not immune to the slowdown in Chinese and American demand for handbags and champagne. None of that changes who runs the group. Shareholders vote on the conversion and merger at extraordinary general meetings in December; if approved, the new Agache SCA structure takes effect at year-end, with the minority tender following in the first quarter of 2027.

hsbc-downgrades-twilio.headline: HSBC downgrade sends Twilio shares tumbling
hsbc-downgrades-twilio.body_md:
Twilio shares fell 6.8% on Friday to $279.36 after HSBC cut its rating on the communications-software firm to Reduce from Hold, breaking with a Wall Street consensus that has otherwise turned more bullish in recent days.

The move stands out less for its rarity — single-firm downgrades happen every week — than for its timing and its argument. Twilio stock has surged roughly 30% since September 8, when Meta's new consumer AI agent, Muse, launched and set off a scramble among investors to identify infrastructure winners. The stock has nearly tripled over the past year. Just three days before HSBC's call, TD Cowen raised its price target to $300 from $260 and Rosenblatt lifted its own to $290 from $275 — both firms reiterating Buy ratings on the same AI-agent thesis that HSBC now says has run too far.

![Twilio logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c0/Twilio_logo.png)

## The bear case, in specifics

HSBC analyst Sameer Lam held his price target at $211 — more than $40 below the Street's average of $254.59 — while downgrading the stock two notches. His argument is not that Muse is a nonevent for Twilio. It's that the market has misjudged which parts of the business benefit.

Investors, Lam argues, have started treating Twilio as the plumbing behind Muse and similar consumer AI agents, and have priced in a share of the upside to match. His view is that Meta keeps the most lucrative layer — the proprietary voice technology — in house, leaving Twilio to handle the commodity work: phone number routing and standard SMS verification, the kind of business that has always carried thin margins. More message volume, in other words, doesn't necessarily mean more profit for Twilio if the messages routed are the low-margin kind.

## Why one downgrade moved the stock this much

A rating change from a single bank rarely produces a near-7% one-day move on its own. What made this one land is the gap it exposes: Twilio's rally has been built substantially on a narrative — that AI agents will drive a new class of premium, Twilio-priced traffic — rather than on disclosed contract terms or updated revenue guidance from Twilio itself. HSBC's note is the first widely circulated attempt to price that narrative against the mechanics of how Muse-driven traffic actually reaches Twilio's network, and it landed on a stock trading at a level that left little room for a competing read to be ignored.

That also means the disagreement is falsifiable in a way vague sentiment shifts are not. If Twilio's next earnings report shows message volumes rising alongside average revenue per message, HSBC's low-margin-plumbing thesis weakens. If volumes rise while margins stay flat or compress, the bulls at TD Cowen and Rosenblatt will have some explaining to do.

## What's next

Twilio does not report third-quarter earnings until late October, which leaves nearly a month in which the stock's direction depends on positioning and further analyst commentary rather than company data. Investors weighing the two camps have, for now, only Lam's routing argument on one side and the broader AI-agent enthusiasm reflected in TD Cowen's and Rosenblatt's targets on the other — a genuine split in view, not a pile-on.

boe-gilts-breeden-hike-signal.headline: Gilt yields hold near multi-year highs as BoE flags November hike, unwinds bond stockpile
boe-gilts-breeden-hike-signal.body_md:
UK gilt yields eased a touch this week but are still camped near territory not seen since before the financial crisis. The 10-year yield stood at 5.35% on Friday, down slightly from a peak closer to 5.4% earlier in the week, but well above the 5.295% it hit on 10 September — itself the highest level since 2007. The reason yields won't come down in any lasting way has less to do with bond supply than with what the Bank of England is expected to do with interest rates in November.

**In one sentence:** Gilt yields eased slightly to 5.35% but remain near 19-year highs as a Bank of England policy shift on QT and hawkish rate signals pull in opposite directions.

## A softer touch on the bond stockpile

At its meeting on 16 September, the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6–3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% — with chief economist Huw Pill and external members Catherine Mann and Megan Greene pushing for an immediate rise to 4%. Alongside that, the Bank announced a significant overhaul of quantitative tightening: the pace of balance-sheet reduction drops from roughly £70bn a year to £46bn, of which only £20bn will come from active gilt sales, the rest from bonds simply maturing. More striking, the Bank paused all gilt sales outright until April 2027 while it consults the Treasury and the Debt Management Office on selling stock directly to the DMO rather than through market auctions. It also stopped selling the longest-dated gilts entirely, retaining roughly £120bn of paper maturing in 2049 and beyond — partly to back future banknote issuance, partly to stop leaning on a part of the curve that was already under strain.

![Bank of England building on Threadneedle Street, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d4/Bank_of_England_Building%2C_London%2C_UK_-_Diliff.jpg)

The market read this as an Operation Twist of sorts — less supply pressure at the long end, in exchange for a longer overall path to a fully unwound £488bn Asset Purchase Facility by 2034. Thirty-year gilt yields fell around 11-12 basis points on the news; the 10-year eased by 7-8bps. For a few days, quantitative tightening was doing the market's work for it, not against it.

## The rates story pulls the other way

That relief didn't last. On 24 September, two deputy governors reasserted the hawkish case. Sarah Breeden, who oversees financial stability, said it was "increasingly appropriate" for Bank Rate to respond as inflation risks crystallise, warning that "the larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we'll see material second-round effects." Clare Lombardelli, the deputy governor for monetary policy, went further, saying firms' capacity to absorb higher energy bills is limited and that policy is "increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation."

The backdrop is the war in Iran, now in its seventh month, which has kept Brent crude near $107 a barrel and pushed August's headline UK inflation to 3.1%. Ofgem's price cap for October to December rises to £1,723, and the Bank expects it to climb again in the first quarter of 2027. Since the conflict began in late February, gilt yields have risen by more than 80 basis points — more than any other G7 government bond market bar Italy's, and roughly double the increase seen in US Treasuries or German Bunds over the same stretch.

Markets have responded by pricing a November hike at close to 70-80% probability, with a further move by February seen as similarly likely — a sharp turn for a Bank that had been cutting rates earlier in the cycle and now finds itself the outlier as the Federal Reserve continues to ease.

## What it means for positioning

The net effect is a rare split decision: the Bank easing pressure on gilt supply with one hand while its own deputies talk up the odds of tighter policy with the other. For sterling, the higher-yield story has not translated into support — GBP/USD has struggled to hold gains even as gilt yields climbed, with investors treating the rise as compensation for risk rather than a reason to buy the currency. That combination — elevated and volatile gilt yields, a central bank still hawkish on rates despite easing off on active sales, and a currency that isn't rewarded for any of it — is the shape of UK duration risk heading into the Bank's next decision on 5 November, when the market will find out whether Breeden and Lombardelli's rhetoric becomes a vote.

trump-federal-film-tax-credit.headline: Trump calls for federal film and TV production tax credit
trump-federal-film-tax-credit.body_md:
President Trump's call for a federal tax credit on film and television production has done something Washington rarely manages on entertainment policy: it has both parties agreeing, and a industry-commissioned study to point to.

A study released September 15 and commissioned by the Motion Picture Association projects that a federal production incentive could add more than 143,000 jobs and lift U.S. production spending by $125 billion by 2035 — pushing total annual spending to $277.5 billion from a projected $152.2 billion without one. Charles Rivkin, the MPA's chairman and chief executive, called the prospect "a gamechanger for our industry," one that would touch "people in all 50 states."

The timing matters. Trump posted his support on Truth Social in early September, urging "Republicans and Democrats" to "immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America" — a pivot from his earlier threat of tariffs on foreign-made films toward a subsidy instead. Los Angeles County has shed more than 40,000 entertainment-sector jobs since 2022, as studios chase cheaper labor and richer incentives in the UK, Canada, Australia and elsewhere. Sixty-five countries now offer some form of film tax credit, according to the MPA study.

![Hollywood sign, Los Angeles](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b0/Hollywood_Sign.JPG)

## The bill taking shape

 Legislation is already drafted. The Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced with bipartisan sponsors — Reps. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Linda Sánchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA) and Laura Friedman (D-CA) in the House, Sens. Tim Scott (R-SC) and Adam Schiff (D-CA) in the Senate — sets a base 20% transferable credit on U.S.-resident labor costs, including post-production and visual effects. Add-ons could push the effective rate to 30%: a 5% bonus for independent productions, another 5% for filming substantially in rural opportunity zones or federally declared disaster areas, and a further uplift for productions that spread work across ten or more states. Eligible productions must cost more than $1 million and film at least 75% of principal photography days domestically; live sports, talk shows, news and corporate video are excluded. The MPA's modelling assumes an effective date of January 1, 2027.

Rep. Friedman put the political framing bluntly: the bill "tells every country that has been outbidding us for American work that we are done losing."

## States, already exposed, brace to compete twice

The harder question for markets is what a federal credit does to the 35-plus states that already run their own incentive programs, several of which have just expanded them. California's new Tax Credit Program 4.0 raised its base credit to a refundable 35–45% of qualified spend, with a $750 million annual cap. New York lifted its program to $800 million, with a 30% base rate plus a 10% upstate bonus. Georgia runs an uncapped 20–30% transferable credit. North Carolina recently tripled its per-project caps. None of that legislative activity looks like a retreat in the face of federal competition — it looks like states hedging in case the federal credit stacks on top of, rather than replaces, their own.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, no natural ally of the administration, responded to Trump's post with "Amen! Let's make it happen," and had floated his own $7.5 billion federal-credit concept months earlier, modelled on California's state program. The convergence is notable: a Democratic governor whose state has borne the brunt of production flight and a Republican president who spent much of the year threatening tariffs on foreign-made films now backing the same subsidy-based fix.

## What it means for capital allocation

For studios and streamers, a federal credit would not replace the location math so much as add a new variable to it — a national floor incentive stacked under whatever state or country program a project also qualifies for. That raises the return threshold state incentive offices need to clear to keep marginal productions from moving anyway, and it gives production accountants a federal baseline to build models around before committing budgets. It also shifts some of the fiscal cost of competing for production activity from state treasuries to the federal one, at a moment when Washington is already running large deficits.

The bill now heads toward the House Ways and Means Committee, where the details — rate levels, caps, the disaster-zone and multi-state uplifts — will be negotiated line by line. The MPA study's 2027 effective-date assumption is aggressive for a tax bill that hasn't yet had a committee markup; the next marker to watch is whether Ways and Means schedules one before year-end.

russia-strikes-ukraine-data-centres.headline: Russia widens attacks on Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, Zelensky says
russia-strikes-ukraine-data-centres.body_md:
The strike came at the end of a week Kyiv had already spent without reliable internet. On Friday, a Russian drone hit the Inkom business centre in the capital's Solomianskyi district, killing four people and tearing into a data centre operated by Datagroup, one of Ukraine's larger telecoms firms. It was not an isolated hit. Two days earlier, on September 23 and 24, Russian Geran-5 attack drones — a jet-powered, long-range design derived from Iran's Shahed — had already struck a cluster of data centres and internet exchange points across the city, cutting service to roughly 100,000 households in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, with knock-on outages reaching Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi.

President Volodymyr Zelensky framed the pattern as deliberate. "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers — for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target," he wrote, adding that the attacks affect "people's ability to stay connected, study, work." He said he had since discussed "additional decisions" with defence officials to harden critical communications infrastructure — though he offered no specifics on what that would involve.

![Volodymyr Zelensky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b1/Volodymyr_Zelensky_Official_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A new column on the target list

Ukraine's internet backbone has, until recently, sat somewhat apart from the war's main axes of destruction — the power grid, the railways, the heating plants that Russia has bombed methodically through three previous winters. That appears to be changing. Over the two days of strikes, Russian forces hit UTELS' switching facility, the CityHost and MiroHost data centres, the Pavutyna network hub, and a central traffic-exchange point used by New-Telco and United DC — the latter two named explicitly by Russia's defence ministry, which claimed they carried military intelligence and security-service traffic. Those claims could not be independently verified. Kyivstar and Parkovyi were also affected, according to Ukrainian officials.

At the 1-IX internet exchange point, engineer Anatolii Frolenkov described a shift in intent rather than just intensity: "This is the beginning of a phase where, since September, they have started taking it out systematically." Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, was blunter, telling reporters Russia had "targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information... it is not a military target."

The human cost has run alongside the infrastructural one. Separately from Friday's four deaths, a 14-year-old Israeli citizen was killed when a residential building was hit in the Pecherskyi district, and Kyiv's mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko, put the total injured from the overnight barrage at 59. In at least one case the disruption compounded the danger directly: outages knocked out air-raid alert systems for some of the 100,000 affected households, meaning the same strikes that severed connectivity also silenced the warning network for whatever came next.

## Resilience, at a cost

What has kept Kyiv from a full blackout is architecture built for exactly this contingency. Oleksandr Olshanskyi, founder of MiroHost — one of the data centres hit, and by his own account 90–95% destroyed in the strike — put the physics plainly: "Destroying all internet in a simple way is impossible — you'd have to use nuclear or chemical weapons or destroy 70–80% of buildings in Kyiv." He added that the intent looked less like military necessity than psychological pressure: "The enemy's goal is to cause damage, inflame panic, and heighten nervousness."

![Aerial view of Kyiv](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/24/Aerial_view_of_Kiev.jpg)

That resilience is itself the product of years of quiet capital reallocation. Olshanskyi said roughly 95% of MiroHost's clients now run infrastructure abroad or in the cloud, insulated from anything short of a strike on a foreign data centre. Most providers restored service within hours to a day, aided by network decentralization — Datagroup, for instance, rerouted traffic across other facilities to bring Friday's outage down to about two hours. But redundancy of this kind isn't free: it means duplicated hosting costs, foreign cloud contracts paid in hard currency, and physical assets at home that insurers increasingly have to price as war-zone risk rather than ordinary commercial property. Each repaired data centre is also a repeat customer for reconstruction financing that Ukraine's private sector has to source largely on its own, since war-risk coverage for digital infrastructure remains thin even among international insurers still willing to write policies in the country.

## What the shift signals

The pivot toward data centres and internet providers fits a broader pattern of Russian strikes moving up the list of civilian-facing targets as the battlefield stalemates and winter approaches — echoing the energy-grid campaigns of prior years, but aimed now at the digital plumbing of a wartime economy that runs increasingly on remote work, digital banking and cloud services. For companies operating in or servicing Ukraine, the practical read is that connectivity, not just power, now belongs on the list of infrastructure that can vanish overnight, with implications for how outsourcing contracts, insurance terms and even foreign-investment decisions get written.

The next test comes as Kyiv moves into its fourth wartime winter: whether Russia pairs strikes on data centres with the kind of coordinated grid attacks seen in 2022 and 2023, which would multiply the strain on backup systems already absorbing losses, or whether this remains a narrower campaign against telecoms in isolation. Ukrainian officials say they are examining new protective measures for communications infrastructure; what those entail, and how quickly they can be funded and built, will shape how much of this resilience is repeatable the next time the drones come.

zelensky-patriot-licence-dispute.headline: Zelensky says Trump agreed to Patriot missile production licences; State Department walks claim back
zelensky-patriot-licence-dispute.body_md:
Volodymyr Zelensky has a habit of announcing American commitments before Washington confirms them, and on Friday the pattern repeated itself with a specificity that made it harder to wave away. The Ukrainian president told reporters that Donald Trump had personally assured him, at their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, that Kyiv would be allowed to manufacture its own Patriot interceptor missiles.

> "At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licences for the production of Patriot missiles."

Within hours, the State Department was contradicting him. Asked to confirm the arrangement, department officials said no final decision had been made — echoing a nearly identical line they had given the German outlet DW just two days earlier, on September 23, when they said discussions on production licences were "continuing." The White House, for its part, has not independently confirmed Zelensky's account either way.

![President Trump greets President Zelensky at the White House, February 2025](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/53/Donald_Trump_and_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_of_Ukraine_with_JD_Vance_and_Marco_Rubio_on_Friday%2C_28_February_2025_at_the_White_House%2C_USA.jpg)

**In one sentence:** Zelensky said Trump personally approved licences for Ukraine to build Patriot missiles; the State Department said no such decision has actually been made.

## A promise that keeps almost happening

This is not the first time the two men have appeared to reach, and then unreach, this exact agreement. Trump first floated the idea publicly at the NATO summit in Ankara in July, calling it "pretty cool" that Ukraine might build its own interceptors. Weeks later he pulled back, saying Washington had to be "very careful" about handing over the underlying technology — sensitive missile-guidance and manufacturing know-how that the US has historically guarded even from close allies.

Then, on July 23, Zelensky announced in Kyiv that Ukraine and Raytheon, the Patriot's manufacturer, had agreed to pursue joint production, with the PAC-2 GEM-T variant reportedly the likeliest candidate and a start date no earlier than late 2027. That announcement, too, ran ahead of any formal US government sign-off. Friday's claim is the third iteration of essentially the same story: a presidential nod in a private conversation, followed by an administration that won't put its name to it in public.

The caution is not simply bureaucratic foot-dragging. Patriot production licences would mean transferring genuine industrial secrets — components, quality-control processes, radar and interceptor design details — to a country still at war, one whose factories are themselves targets for Russian strikes on energy and infrastructure. Any US administration would weigh that risk carefully, and the Trump White House's approach to Ukraine policy has run hot and cold enough that hesitation at the working level, even after an apparent presidential green light, is plausible.

## Why Kyiv needs this now

The timing gives Zelensky's account weight even if it turns out premature. Ukraine's Patriot batteries have been consuming interceptors far faster than they can be replaced. Estimates put routine monthly usage at 60 to 70 missiles, rising to 150–180 during concentrated Russian ballistic-missile barrages — output that a global production base already strained by the US-Iran conflict, which reportedly burned through more than two years' worth of global Patriot interceptor manufacturing, cannot easily match. Zelensky said in August that Ukraine needs roughly 5% of the US interceptor stockpile just to survive the coming winter, and 10% to neutralise Russia's ballistic missile arsenal outright.

A domestic production line, even a partial one, would ease that dependency over time — though industry estimates suggest any Ukrainian facility would need over a year to reach meaningful output, meaning the licence itself would do little to solve this winter's shortage even if granted today.

## What the contradiction signals

The substance of the dispute — whether Ukraine gets a manufacturing licence — matters far less to markets than the pattern it reveals. A US ally's head of state stating, on the record and in direct quotes, that the American president made him a "final decision" commitment, only for the State Department to say otherwise within 48 hours, is not a story about missiles. It is a story about whether anyone outside the Oval Office can reliably describe what US policy toward Ukraine actually is at a given moment.

That uncertainty is precisely what defense investors and geopolitical risk desks price in when they read stories like this one: not the missile technology itself, but the reliability of the signal. Zelensky has strong incentives to over-report American commitments — it reassures a domestic audience worn down by nearly three years of war and pressures Washington into living up to the claim publicly. The State Department has equally strong incentives to hedge — sensitive technology transfers move slowly through interagency review regardless of what gets said in a bilateral meeting. Both dynamics can be true at once, which is exactly why the contradiction keeps recurring rather than resolving.

The next marker to watch is whether the State Department's review produces an actual announcement, rather than another round of "discussions are continuing." Congress would also need to weigh in on any formal export-control or technology-release decision of this scale, giving lawmakers a venue to either ratify or undercut whatever Trump privately told Zelensky. Until one of those institutional steps happens, the safest reading is the State Department's: no final decision, whatever was said in the room in New York.

burnham-election-speculation.headline: Burnham denies early-election plans as Healey appointment and slipping poll numbers fuel Labour tension
burnham-election-speculation.body_md:
Andy Burnham spent Friday doing something politicians rarely do with any conviction: closing a door he had spent the previous fortnight leaving suspiciously ajar. Asked by ITV Calendar whether Britain's next general election would come in 2029, as scheduled, the prime minister did not hedge. "Well, yes, that's when the next election will be," he said, before adding of the swirling Westminster chatter to the contrary: "I can knock that dead."

It was Burnham's first party conference as Labour leader and prime minister, and by his own account it should have been an occasion to talk about government, not electoral arithmetic. That it became the latter says something about how unsettled his position still is, two months after he replaced Keir Starmer in Downing Street.

> "All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead." — Andy Burnham, ITV Calendar

![Prime Minister Andy Burnham](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A denial that answers a question nobody officially asked

Burnham became Labour leader on 17 July and prime minister three days later, after Starmer resigned on 22 June in the face of a collapse in confidence among his own MPs. That is an unusually compressed handover, and it left Burnham without the mandate a general election would confer — a gap that matters more the longer a government goes without renewing it. Speculation that he might close that gap early was not conjured from nothing: Labour has enjoyed a modest bounce in the polls since the leadership change, and a prime minister sitting on rising numbers has an obvious incentive to bank them before they fade.

So when Healey — Chancellor John Healey, formerly defence secretary under Starmer — appointed Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour's 2024 manifesto and helped devise Starmer's five governing "missions," as his senior special adviser, the appointment read to Westminster as a tell. A manifesto author moving into a senior Treasury advisory role is the kind of personnel move a government makes when it is thinking about what it would promise voters next, not merely how it governs now. Burnham's ITV Calendar interview was, in substance if not in form, a direct response to that inference.

![John Healey](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_portrait_of_John_Healey_crop_3.jpg)

The denial matters for reasons beyond Westminster gossip. A fixed election date removes a source of near-term political risk that had begun to price itself, however faintly, into expectations for gilts and UK equities — the prospect of a government seeking a fresh mandate mid-parliament tends to invite policy uncertainty that markets dislike more than almost any specific outcome. By fixing the horizon at 2029, Burnham has taken a tail risk off the table for the next two to three years. It is a defensive move — it calms a fear rather than announcing a plan — but defensive signals still count as information.

## The poll numbers behind the pressure

The timing is not incidental. YouGov's latest MRP model, drawn from nearly 17,000 respondents surveyed between 23 August and 18 September, projects Labour as the largest party on 241 seats, with the Conservatives on 130 and Reform UK — Nigel Farage's party — collapsing to 123. That is a reversal with few precedents in modern British polling: a year earlier, YouGov's equivalent model had put Reform on 311 seats, within striking distance of a majority.

![Nigel Farage](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d7/Official_portrait_of_Nigel_Farage_MP_crop_2.jpg)

Reform still leads on national vote share, according to the same poll — the collapse in its seat count is a function of Britain's first-past-the-post system rather than a collapse in its underlying support. Its vote is spread too evenly across too many seats to convert efficiently into wins, the same geographic dispersion problem that has hobbled third-party insurgencies in the UK for decades. But the seat projection is what MPs act on, and a Reform reduced to third place looks far less like a party any government need fear outflanking. For Labour, that combination — improved standing, a fading Reform threat — makes the case for going early more tempting, not less, which is precisely why Burnham needed to be so emphatic in shutting it down.

## A cabinet split over growth

The conference was also where Labour's other fault line surfaced in public. Peter Kyle, a Starmer ally sacked from cabinet in Burnham's reshuffle upon taking office, told the BBC that the new government was not focused enough on boosting growth and needed to act with "more urgency." Kyle was careful to frame this as something short of criticism — he described himself as "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government" — but the distinction will not travel far. A former cabinet minister publicly urging his successor's government to move faster on the economy, delivered in the run-up to conference, is a rebuke by any name.

![Peter Kyle](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/Official_portrait_of_Peter_Kyle_MP.jpg)

It fits a broader pattern of friction between the Starmer and Burnham wings of the party. One Burnham ally used the eve of conference to accuse Starmer's old operation of overseeing "rot" in Labour; Kyle's intervention was, in effect, the return volley. Burnham became prime minister via his party's collapse in confidence in its previous leader rather than through an election win of his own, and that origin story leaves him more exposed to internal sniping than a leader who arrived via the ballot box. Growth policy is simply the terrain on which that exposure is currently being tested.

## What the pieces add up to

Taken together, the week describes a prime minister managing multiple pressures at once by closing off the one he could most easily control. He cannot immediately silence a rival wing of his own party or dictate how First-Past-the-Post metabolises Reform's vote share, but he can, with one unambiguous sentence to a regional broadcaster, take an early election off the table. That the market-relevant conclusion is what did not happen — no snap poll, no fresh mandate, no manifesto rewrite this side of 2029 — is itself the story. It buys Burnham time against his internal critics without resolving the argument they are having with him, and it leaves the government's economic record, not its electoral tactics, as the metric by which that time will be judged. The next marker is the Autumn Budget, where Kyle's demand for growth "urgency" will either be answered or repeated.

iran-seven-day-hormuz-plan.headline: Iran offers seven-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks
iran-seven-day-hormuz-plan.body_md:
Iran's foreign minister has put a new number on the table: seven days. That is how long Tehran says it would take to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal shipping and sit back down with Washington over its nuclear programme — provided the United States first stops fighting, lifts its naval blockade, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and unfreezes Iranian assets abroad.

Abbas Araghchi laid out the plan at a private gathering on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday, according to people in the room, including Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute think tank. It is the most concrete diplomatic move either side has made since a previous ceasefire fell apart in July, and it arrives as American voters head toward pumps averaging $4.46 a gallon — the highest of the year — seven weeks before the midterm elections.

## What Iran is offering

The mechanics, as described by Araghchi, are sequential rather than simultaneous. Fighting would stop across all fronts, including Lebanon, within the first day or two. Over the following four to five days, the US would be expected to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions restricting Iranian oil exports and guarantee no further strikes. The Strait of Hormuz — the 33-kilometre channel through which roughly a fifth of the world's daily oil supply and a similar share of global LNG normally passes — would reopen on day six. On day seven, Araghchi said, "the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects."

![Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at a meeting with foreign envoys in Tehran, January 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/Iranian_Foreign_Minister_Seyyed_Abbas_Araghchi_12th_January_2026.jpg)

That ordering is the crux of the dispute. Iran wants the strait settled first and the nuclear question addressed afterward, as a separate track. The Trump administration has insisted the opposite: that Hormuz, sanctions relief and the nuclear file all be negotiated as a single package, with no reopening of the strait until Tehran has made verifiable commitments on enrichment. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's response on Wednesday was carefully noncommittal — "if there's an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will" — which is diplomatic language for *not yet*.

## A second attempt at Islamabad

The proposal is not being read in isolation. It closely mirrors the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed by both presidents on 17 June after an earlier round of fighting, which set a 60-day window to negotiate a final settlement and included its own — vaguer — provisions on the strait. That agreement collapsed within three weeks. On 7 July, Iranian forces struck three commercial vessels transiting Hormuz, including a Qatari LNG tanker that caught fire, after accusing them of ignoring Iran's approved shipping routes. Washington answered with airstrikes on Iranian territory within a day, and the ceasefire was effectively dead.

![Map of the Strait of Hormuz, the channel connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/Strait_of_Hormuz-svg-en.svg)

The US then imposed its own naval blockade and began charging shipping companies for safe-passage guarantees, on top of the disruption Iran's attacks had already caused. Traffic through the strait, which normally runs at 88 to 130 vessel transits a day, fell to roughly ten on a single day counted in late July. The International Energy Agency has called the resulting disruption the largest in the history of the global oil market. Seven months into the war, the compressed seven-day version of the Islamabad script looks less like a fresh idea than an attempt to salvage the old one before it is forgotten entirely — this time with a tighter clock and, Iranian officials hope, more urgent politics on the American side.

## The politics behind the clock

That urgency is deliberate. Parsi, who relayed Araghchi's private remarks, said the foreign minister suggested a fast deal would hand President Trump a win before the midterms: lower pump prices, an end to a war that has dragged on far longer than promised, and a nuclear track he could still claim credit for shaping. "If Trump calculates this arrangement is worthwhile and can bring political benefit before the midterms and reduce gas prices, perhaps we'll see flexibility not seen in previous weeks," Parsi said — while cautioning that deep mutual suspicion remains, including US concern that Iran wants the breathing room chiefly to sell more oil and ease its own economic strain.

![Official portrait of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/31/Official_portrait_of_Secretary_Marco_Rubio_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Trump has publicly rejected the idea that the electoral calendar drives his Iran policy, telling reporters this month that gas prices would fall only "right after" the midterms and that the war would end "immediately after the election." On the underlying trade-off, he has been blunt: elevated prices are "a very inexpensive price to pay" for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, he said in September — a line unlikely to reassure voters who have watched pump prices climb toward $6 a gallon in California. Whether that political calculus shifts is precisely what Araghchi appears to be betting on.

## What would actually move markets

For oil markets, the distinction between a real sequencing breakthrough and another failed memorandum matters more than the seven-day framing itself. Brent crude jumped more than 9% in a single session in July when the US blockade was announced; a credible reopening of Hormuz, verified by tanker movements rather than communiqués, is the kind of event that could unwind a meaningful share of the war-risk premium now priced into crude and refined products. A repeat of June — vague language, quick collapse, renewed strikes — would do the opposite, reinforcing the view among traders and insurers that Gulf shipping risk is now structural rather than episodic.

Washington has not formally responded to the seven-day plan, and Rubio's guarded comment suggests no immediate answer is coming. The next marker to watch is whether the two sides establish direct contact at working level in New York before the General Assembly session closes, and whether Trump — with midterms now under two months away — signals any willingness to decouple Hormuz from the nuclear file, the sequencing gap that sank the last deal and is blocking this one.

ftc-ai-agents-anthropomorphising.headline: FTC chair vows to keep resisting 'anthropomorphising' of AI agents
ftc-ai-agents-anthropomorphising.body_md:
Andrew Ferguson, the Federal Trade Commission's chairman, spent part of a stage appearance in Austin this week doing something regulators rarely bother with: talking down the very technology his agency is supposed to police.

Speaking at the Reuters Momentum AI conference on September 25, Ferguson said he would keep pushing back against the habit — common among AI companies and journalists alike — of describing software agents as if they have minds of their own. "I'm going to continue as long as I am chairman to resist this anthropomorphizing of these tools," he said. His argument: when an AI agent does something harmful, the fault lies with whoever built or instructed it, not with the tool itself. "If someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don't think we would say, 'Oh, what do we do about the tool?'"

It's a jab at a narrative that has gained currency as AI firms describe systems occasionally acting in unexpected ways. Ferguson said that when the FTC has looked at audit trails in such cases, the systems were simply carrying out the instructions they'd been given — not breaking loose with, in his phrase, "wills and desires of their own." The practical upshot is a liability theory: developers and deployers, not the code, sit in the FTC's crosshairs.

## Where the FTC is actually looking

The philosophical point was really a setup for the news. Asked where he personally worries most about AI's effect on consumers, Ferguson named three sectors: delivery apps, rideshare services and airlines. All three have faced years of suspicion that pricing algorithms tailor fares and fees to what a given customer — or a given moment of demand — will bear, rather than posting one price for everyone.

Airlines have particular reason to feel the heat. Delta Air Lines drew criticism last year after an executive suggested the carrier was using AI tools to help gauge how much individual customers were willing to pay for a ticket, a comment that reignited long-running fears about "personalized pricing" in air travel. Ferguson's comments suggest that episode has stuck with regulators.

He said the FTC plans to request data directly from companies in these sectors as part of a forthcoming study, and that the agency "would not hesitate" to bring enforcement action where firms use personalized or algorithmic pricing without disclosing it to consumers. That is a narrower ask than a crackdown on the practice itself — dynamic pricing is legal, and airlines have used yield-management software for decades. The line the FTC is drawing is around disclosure: whether customers know a price was shaped by their own data.

## A regulator picking its lane

Ferguson has been consistent in arguing the FTC should not become a general-purpose AI regulator without Congress telling it to. Instead, he has framed the agency's role as applying existing consumer-protection and data-security law to specific harms — deceptive claims, undisclosed data use, breaches — wherever AI happens to be involved. That includes, he suggested, treating a company's failure to disclose a data breach caused by an AI agent the same way the FTC would treat any other breach disclosure failure.

The anthropomorphizing comments and the pricing comments are, in that sense, two sides of the same position: don't treat the AI as a novel legal subject, and don't treat AI-enabled pricing as a novel legal problem either. Both, in Ferguson's telling, reduce to conduct by companies that existing law already covers.

## What comes next

The near-term step is the data request to delivery, rideshare and airline operators, which will feed into an FTC study rather than an immediate enforcement action — Ferguson was careful to frame this as an ongoing area of focus, not a new case. For companies like DoorDash, Uber, Lyft and the major carriers, the practical question is how their pricing algorithms document and disclose the data they use, since that is where Ferguson says the agency's attention — and any future action — will land.

miliband-warns-iran-minister.headline: Miliband warns Iran minister UK 'will not tolerate' hostile activity on British soil
miliband-warns-iran-minister.body_md:
The photograph is what everyone will remember: Ed Miliband, Britain's foreign secretary, shaking the hand of Abbas Araghchi, Iran's foreign minister, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. But the substance of the encounter, held on Thursday, was a pointed warning — delivered face to face, in the room, rather than through a diplomatic note.

Miliband told Araghchi that the UK "will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil," according to the Foreign Office, and specifically raised suspected Iranian links to attacks on Britain's Jewish community, including an incident over Rosh Hashanah at Lauderdale Road Synagogue in Maida Vale, where hooded youths set off fireworks. He also urged Araghchi to pursue "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" — a reference to the wider Iran-Israel-US conflict — and pressed for the release of Craig and Lindsay Foreman, the British couple sentenced to ten years in Tehran on espionage charges they deny.

![Ed Miliband](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Secretary_of_State_for_Energy_Security_and_Net_Zero_Ed_Miliband_%2855066031341%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

> "Not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil — including attacks on the British Jewish community."

## A pattern, not a single incident

The warning did not come out of nowhere. MI5's director-general, Ken McCallum, told an audience last October that the service had tracked more than twenty potentially lethal Iran-backed plots on British soil in a single year — a run of assassination and kidnap attempts against dissidents, journalists and Jewish community targets that has been building since 2022. The Foreman case has simmered in the background for 20 months, a recurring irritant in a relationship that Miliband's own department has tried, since his appointment by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July, to manage rather than sever entirely.

What's missing from Thursday's account is specificity about a trigger. The Foreign Office statement bundles together the synagogue incident, the Foreman detention and the broader pattern of plots without identifying a single new event that prompted this particular warning at this particular meeting. That ambiguity matters for reading the story correctly: this reads as an accumulation of grievances aired in a scheduled diplomatic encounter, not a response to a fresh provocation.

## Immediate reaction, no policy shift

The meeting itself drew swifter and louder reaction than its content. Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign secretary, accused Miliband of "legitimising a regime that has often tried to harm our people," citing Iran's arming of the Houthis and its record against domestic protesters. Alicia Kearns, a shadow Foreign Office minister, went further, calling the encounter a "propaganda win for the Iranians" and saying Miliband "owes Parliament, British Jews, and the Foreman family an explanation."

Araghchi, for his part, used the meeting to press Iran's own grievance — telling Miliband that Britain, France and Germany should be "held accountable" for failing to take a firm stance against what Tehran calls the US-Israeli war on Iran. There is no indication either side left with anything concrete: no new sanctions, no announced security measures, no Iranian commitment on the Foremans. The Foreign Office also confirmed the pair discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for global oil shipments, though again without any resulting agreement.

## What to watch

The test of whether Thursday's language amounts to anything is whether it is followed by action — new sanctions designations, a change in the Foremans' case, or a formal MI5 briefing tying a specific plot to Tehran. Absent that, the exchange sits alongside a long run of similar UK warnings to Iran: firm in tone, thin on consequence.

fbi-shinyhunters-breach.headline: FBI hacked by ShinyHunters; personal data on thousands of agents allegedly stolen
fbi-shinyhunters-breach.body_md:
The FBI is investigating a claim that has become depressingly familiar in 2026: an extortion gang says it walked into a federal system through unpatched enterprise software, and walked out with terabytes of data on the people who work there.

The group calling itself ShinyHunters told the security outlet BleepingComputer it exploited a previously unknown vulnerability — a zero-day — in Oracle PeopleSoft, the human-resources and applicant-tracking software many large organizations use to manage employee records. From there, the group says it moved laterally into FBI-managed infrastructure hosted on Amazon's GovCloud, the segregated cloud region built for US government workloads, and pulled between 2 and 3 terabytes of data. A sample reviewed by 404 Media reportedly includes records on roughly 5,000 agents.

The FBI has not confirmed a breach occurred. A spokesperson told TechCrunch only that the bureau "is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating." That carefully hedged language is standard for an active investigation, but it leaves the core claims — the zero-day, the scope, the GovCloud pivot — resting entirely on the word of the people who broke in.

## What was allegedly taken

ShinyHunters says the haul spans records tied to the FBI's human-resources, criminal-justice and Medlink systems — the last of these covering medical evaluations for agents and applicants. Beyond names, the group claims to have home addresses and phone numbers, in some cases extending to agents' spouses.

![The J. Edgar Hoover Building, FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/10/FBI_Headquarters_-_J._Edgar_Hoover_Building_%2853840035941%29_b.jpg)

That combination matters more than a typical customer-data leak. Home addresses of law-enforcement personnel are the raw material for swatting and physical intimidation — tactics ShinyHunters itself has been accused of using against its victims. Medical evaluation records, meanwhile, are exactly the kind of leverage a hostile intelligence service would want on an officer it hoped to coerce or discredit. Security researchers told Axios the incident appears consistent with a genuine intrusion, even though none of the technical specifics — the zero-day, the exfiltration volume — have been independently verified by outside firms.

## An oddly personal motive

What sets this apart from ShinyHunters' usual playbook is the stated reason for it. The group has spent the past two years running a criminal ecosystem — sometimes overlapping with Scattered Spider and Lapsus\$ under the banner "Scattered Lapsus\$ Hunters" — built on data theft and extortion, from the 2024 Snowflake customer breaches to the 2025 wave of Salesforce and Salesloft intrusions that touched more than 700 organizations. Those campaigns were financially motivated: pay up, or the data goes public.

This one, the group insists, is not about money. It says the attack is retaliation for an FBI FLASH advisory issued in the second quarter of 2026 that described ShinyHunters' harassment tactics — including threats and swatting against victims and their families — and urged targets not to pay ransoms. ShinyHunters is demanding the bureau retract the advisory within a week. Whether or not that demand is met, the episode shows an extortion group treating a law-enforcement warning as a personal insult worth burning capability over — using a zero-day, rather than selling or hoarding it, purely to make a point.

## The Oracle problem, again

The more durable story here may be about the software, not the attackers. This is not Oracle's first bad year. In October 2025, the Cl0p ransomware group exploited a separate zero-day — CVE-2025-61882, with a maximum-severity CVSS score of 9.8 — in Oracle E-Business Suite, another enterprise resource-planning product, compromising at least 103 organizations across finance, manufacturing and the public sector before CISA forced an emergency patch deadline. PeopleSoft and E-Business Suite are both decades-old Oracle application suites that remain embedded in government and corporate back offices precisely because they are hard to rip out.

![Oracle's former corporate headquarters in Redwood Shores, California.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Oracle_Headquarters_Redwood_Shores.jpg)

Oracle has not yet issued a statement on the ShinyHunters claim; the company was contacted by multiple outlets, including TechCrunch and BleepingComputer, and has not responded publicly as of this writing. If a second Oracle zero-day in a year turns out to be real, it hands regulators and federal auditors a pattern rather than an isolated incident — and a harder question about why systems handling agents' home addresses and medical files were reachable from the internet at all.

## What's next

The FBI's investigation is the near-term catalyst: confirmation or denial of the zero-day, the AWS GovCloud pivot, and the true scope of the data taken would settle a story that currently runs entirely on the attackers' own claims. Watch also for whether Oracle issues a patch or advisory for PeopleSoft — the kind of disclosure that would, on its own, corroborate ShinyHunters' account regardless of what the bureau says. And if ShinyHunters' one-week deadline passes without the FBI retracting its advisory, the next move — quiet or loud — will say a good deal about whether this was retaliation for its own sake or the opening move in something with a price tag attached.

el-nino-food-security-risk.headline: El Niño intensification raises drought and flood risk across key food-producing regions
el-nino-food-security-risk.body_md:
The UN's World Meteorological Organization says the El Niño now building in the Pacific has an almost 100% chance of persisting through February 2027 and could become one of the strongest on record — a forecast so unequivocal that WMO chief Celeste Saulo said it was the first time the agency had issued an El Niño update with this degree of certainty. UN Secretary-General António Guterres put it more bluntly: "El Niño is being supersized before our eyes."

For traders in wheat, corn and soy futures, the forecast matters less as a weather story than as a repricing signal. El Niño shifts rainfall and temperature patterns across the world's grain belts in fairly predictable ways, and the scale of this one raises the odds that at least one major producing region takes a real hit to yields just as global stockpiles are already stretched thin by years of climate volatility.

![Corn showing the effects of drought in Navasota, Texas](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a1/Corn_shows_the_effect_of_drought.jpg)

## Where the risk concentrates

The Niño 3.4 index — the standard measure of Pacific warming — averaged 1.5°C above normal from May to July, hit 2°C in July, and peaked near 2.6°C in August, with some subsurface Pacific waters running 8°C above normal. WMO's models point to above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire land surface of the planet through November, layered on rainfall patterns that follow the classic El Niño script: flooding in some places, drought in others.

The UN Food and Agriculture Organization has flagged Southeast Asia's rice belt as particularly exposed. India, Vietnam and Thailand — the world's three largest rice exporters — are among the countries most likely to see planting and yields disrupted. In East Africa, forecasters expect a two-stage pattern: drought curtailing crops in Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan, Uganda and western Kenya through the northern autumn, followed by a flood-inducing deluge toward year-end. Southern Africa faces its own heat-and-drought risk. South America's picture is more mixed — Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru are expecting above-average rain, which forecasters say could lift South American soybean output even as it complicates Brazil's planting calendar and shortens the window for its second corn crop.

The U.S. Corn Belt is, for now, the outlier. Warmer, wetter conditions forecast for the Midwest could support rather than threaten yields, and some analysts expect U.S. soybean and hard red winter wheat prices to soften if that plays out. Durum wheat is a different matter: the EU's Joint Research Centre has warned that a strong El Niño scenario could push global durum prices higher regardless of what happens in North America.

## The market and humanitarian response

FAO and the World Food Programme have already launched their first-ever joint anticipatory action appeal tied to an El Niño event, seeking $202 million to protect 8.8 million people across 22 high-risk countries — funding cash transfers, drought-tolerant and flood-resistant seed, livestock support and flood defences before the worst of the disruption lands. The agencies estimate every dollar spent this way avoids roughly seven dollars in later losses. UN officials separately project nearly 50 million additional people could face acute hunger as the event unfolds.

For commodity desks, the signal is less about any single number than about dispersion: a strong El Niño tends to widen the range of outcomes across regions and crops simultaneously, which is precisely the condition that lifts hedging demand and options volatility even before a single harvest is in trouble. Markets have been here before — the 2015-16 and 2023-24 events both produced sharp, short-lived spikes in agricultural futures — but WMO's own comparison points are the ones from 1997-98 and 2015-16, both among the most disruptive on record.

Scientists caution that human-caused warming has not been shown to intensify El Niño itself, but it does amplify what the event delivers, since warmer oceans and a hotter atmosphere hold more heat and moisture to feed both the droughts and the floods. Researchers have not established that El Niño's frequency or strength is increasing at all, only that when the naturally occurring the event does not is the process of intensification.

The next marker to watch is WMO's updated outlook expected in December, when the event's trajectory into its northern-hemisphere-winter peak should become clearer — along with the first real read on how Southeast Asia's rice harvest and Brazil's planting season are holding up.

manston-inquiry-home-office-policy.headline: Manston asylum inquiry hears overcrowding and racism linked to Home Office policy, as ex-ministers face questions
manston-inquiry-home-office-policy.body_md:
Four years on from the boat crossings that overwhelmed it, the Manston asylum processing centre in Kent is back in the news — this time in a hearing room, not a headline about queues on the beach. The independent inquiry into what happened at the site in autumn 2022 held its second preliminary hearing on Friday, and the picture emerging is not one of a system buckling under unforeseeable pressure. It is one of choices made, and remade, at the top of government.

Manston was built to hold up to 1,600 new arrivals for a maximum of 24 hours — a triage point, not a shelter. By November 2022 it was holding roughly 4,000 people, some for as long as 33 days. Counsel to the inquiry, Claire Dobbin KC, has told hearings that sixty families were crammed into eleven rooms in a barracks block with no hot water or showers, and that at points 81 people — babies, children, teenagers, adults — shared a single toilet. There was no soap. Diphtheria spread among detainees. The inquiry has also heard that "very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff," alongside allegations of people being locked in isolation vans as punishment and detainees attempting self-harm with barbed wire.

One death sits at the centre of the case: Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, a 31-year-old Iraqi man, fell ill with diphtheria and was, according to evidence heard so far, kept in handcuffs in hospital until roughly two and a half hours before he died.

## Not an accident, a decision

What distinguishes this inquiry from a routine post-mortem of an administrative failure is where the evidence points. Witnesses have described Number 10 as having "clearly played a decision-making role" in pausing transfers of asylum seekers from Manston into hotel accommodation — the very decision that let the population balloon past anything the site could hold. That reframes the crisis: not a logistics failure overtaken by an unexpected surge in Channel crossings, but the foreseeable result of a policy choice to keep people on site rather than move them on, made and sustained at ministerial level.

![The Home Office headquarters at 2 Marsham Street, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d8/Home_Office%2C_2_Marsham_Street%2C_London.jpg)

That is why the witness list reads like a Conservative cabinet reunion. Chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, the inquiry expects to hear from three former home secretaries — Priti Patel, Suella Braverman and Grant Shapps — plus former immigration minister Robert Jenrick, five other ex-immigration ministers, and former prime ministers Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak, both in office at different points during the 2022 crisis. Dobbin has said the conditions in which children were held "raise very serious questions" about what ministers were prepared to tolerate.

## What's next

Cartwright has confirmed only that directions following Friday's hearing will set a start date, venue and witness timetable for the substantive oral hearings — the point at which Patel, Braverman and the rest will actually be questioned under oath. Separately, Home Office officials have already been charged with conspiracy to steal and misconduct in public office over conduct at the site. Between the criminal case and the inquiry's eventual findings, Manston is shaping up as a rare instance where a chaotic news cycle from 2022 gets a formal, on-the-record reckoning — one that could yet reach further than a single facility's failings, into the machinery of who signs off on policies that leave people penned in barracks with one toilet between eighty-one.
